questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with painless ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. On examination there is a single, clean-based ulcer with indurated edges and a rubbery feel. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged but non-tender. Dark-field microscopy is the best diagnostic test. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: This is classic primary syphilis (chancre): painless indurated ulcer with rubbery non-tender lymphadenopathy. Caused by Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy of ulcer exudate is the gold standard for diagnosis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent patient develops multiple vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome on the right side with severe burning pain. The most appropriate first-line antiviral therapy is:
opts: Both B and C are equally appropriate
questions.exp: Herpes zoster is treated with antivirals within 72 hours of rash onset. Valacyclovir 1000 mg TDS or Famciclovir 500 mg TDS for 7 days are preferred over Acyclovir for better bioavailability and simpler dosing. Acyclovir for zoster requires 800 mg 5 times/day.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic presents with rapidly spreading cellulitis of the right leg with bullae formation, crepitus on palpation, and wooden-hard texture of the skin. Blood cultures show gram-positive cocci in chains. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis type II (Streptococcal NF) is caused by Group A Streptococcus (gram-positive cocci in chains). Features include rapid spread, bullae, crepitus, wooden-hard skin, and systemic toxicity. Urgent surgical debridement is life-saving.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the trunk and extremities for 6 months. Slit-skin smear shows acid-fast bacilli with a bacteriological index of 4+. Which type of leprosy does this represent?
questions.exp: A bacteriological index (BI) of 4+ indicates high bacillary load, consistent with Lepromatous leprosy (LL). In LL, the immune response is poor, bacilli multiply freely (BI 4-6+), and lesions are numerous, symmetrical, and poorly defined.

questions.q: A 30-year-old female with known systemic lupus erythematosus develops tense bullae on normal and inflamed skin, predominantly on the trunk. Immunofluorescence shows IgG deposits at the dermal-epidermal junction in a linear pattern. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous SLE presents with tense subepidermal blisters and linear IgG (also IgA, IgM, complement) deposits at DEJ on DIF. The target antigen is type VII collagen (same as EBA). It occurs in patients with active SLE and responds dramatically to dapsone.

questions.q: A patient is receiving chemotherapy and develops painful oral erosions, target lesions on palms and soles, and conjunctival injection. Skin biopsy shows necrotic keratinocytes and subepidermal cleavage with 30% BSA involvement. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: TEN involves >30% BSA epidermal detachment; SJS involves <10% BSA; SJS-TEN overlap involves 10-30%. The presence of necrotic keratinocytes and subepidermal split is characteristic of TEN/SJS spectrum. Chemotherapy drugs can trigger TEN.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales on the extensor surfaces and scalp for 5 years. He now develops joint pain and stiffness. The seronegative arthritis in psoriasis most commonly affects which joints?
opts: Large joints like knee and hip
questions.exp: Psoriatic arthritis classically involves DIP joints (distinctive from RA) and can involve the axial skeleton causing spondylitis/sacroiliitis. It is seronegative (RF negative). The 5 patterns include DIP joint predominant, oligoarticular, polyarticular, axial, and arthritis mutilans.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male from South India presents with a 2 cm hyperpigmented plaque on the left cheek that has been growing slowly over 10 years. On Wood's lamp examination, pigmentation becomes more pronounced. Dermoscopy shows honeycomb pattern. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Acquired bilateral naevi of Ota-like macules (ABNOM)
questions.exp: Melasma is a common hyperpigmentation in darker skin types. Wood's lamp accentuates epidermal melanin (not dermal). Dermoscopy shows pseudoreticular/honeycomb pattern. Treatment involves photoprotection, hydroquinone, and combination creams.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents with recurrent painful genital ulcers, oral aphthae, and uveitis. She also has a positive pathergy test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is characterized by the triad of recurrent oral aphthae, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Pathergy test (prick test causing papule/pustule at 24-48h) is positive particularly in Middle Eastern and Asian patients.

questions.q: A newborn presents with large fluid-filled bullae at birth, predominantly in areas of trauma. Parents are consanguineous. Electron microscopy shows blister formation within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. Which disease mechanism is most likely?
questions.exp: EB within the lamina lucida is junctional EB. Laminin-332 (previously laminin-5) deficiency causes Herlitz-type junctional EB, the most severe form. Plectin deficiency causes EB with muscular dystrophy. Integrin deficiency causes EB with pyloric atresia. Col VII deficiency causes dystrophic EB (sublamina densa).

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with a chronic non-healing ulcer on the dorsum of the right foot for 2 years. He noticed a painless swelling 5 years ago. There are sinuses discharging white sulfur granules. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Mycetoma (Madura foot) with white sulfur granules is typically caused by Actinomyces israelii or Nocardia (actinomycetoma). Treatment is antibacterial: Streptomycin + co-trimoxazole for 9-12+ months. White granules suggest Actinomycetoma; black granules suggest Eumycetoma (treated with itraconazole/surgery).

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive male with CD4 count 50 cells/mm³ presents with vegetating plaques in the groin, perineum, and perianal area. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and suppurative granulomas with giant cells containing broad-based budding yeast. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Blastomycosis presents with vegetating/verrucous plaques and is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. Histopathology shows broad-based budding yeast (pathognomonic). Cryptococcus shows narrow-based budding. Coccidioides shows spherules with endospores. Histoplasma shows intracellular narrow-based budding.

questions.q: A 65-year-old female presents with itch-free tense bullae predominantly on the flexural areas and lower abdomen. DIF shows linear C3 and IgG deposits along the BMZ. ELISA is positive for BP180 antibody. The best initial treatment is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease with antibodies to BP180 (and BP230). First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day). Super-potent topical corticosteroids (clobetasol) are an alternative for limited disease with fewer systemic side effects.

questions.q: A 19-year-old female presents with pruritic papules and vesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at the dermal papillae tips with subepidermal cleft. She also has malabsorption. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces. Granular IgA deposits at dermal papilla tips are pathognomonic on DIF. It is associated with celiac disease. Treatment is dapsone for rapid relief + lifelong gluten-free diet.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male from Northeast India presents with a slowly progressive nodular lesion on the dorsum of the right hand for 8 months. Biopsy reveals sporotrichoid spread with lymphangitic nodules. Culture on Sabouraud's dextrose agar at 25°C shows dematiaceous colony. The most likely fungal pathogen is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (dark-pigmented) fungi, most commonly Fonsecaea pedrosoi in Asia. It presents with verrucous nodules on extremities. Histopathology shows 'copper-penny sclerotic bodies.' Sporothrix also causes sporotrichoid pattern but is dimorphic (not dematiaceous on SDA at 25°C).

questions.q: A 28-year-old female presents with pain at the nail fold with pus discharge. She works as a housewife and frequently wets her hands. Microbiological culture grows Candida albicans. What is the appropriate management?
opts: Topical clotrimazole + keep the area dry
questions.exp: Candidal paronychia is treated with topical antifungals (clotrimazole, miconazole) and keeping the area dry. Avoiding wet work and using protective gloves is key. Systemic therapy reserved for refractory cases. IV amphotericin is for systemic/disseminated candidiasis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the mouth and nose. Gram stain of pus shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. The child is non-immunocompromised. Most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Topical mupirocin 2% ointment TDS for 5 days
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes. For localized, non-complicated impetigo, topical mupirocin 2% is the first-line treatment (or retapamulin). Oral antibiotics are reserved for extensive/multiple lesions, immunocompromised, or systemic features.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with multiple smooth papules around the eyelids and cheeks. On squeezing, white cheesy material is expressed. Electron microscopy would show a characteristic inclusion: a large cytoplasmic inclusion body occupying most of the cell. What is the causative virus?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus (MCV types 1 and 2). The characteristic pathological feature is Henderson-Paterson bodies (intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies) visible on H&E staining. It presents as pearly, umbilicated papules.

questions.q: During a leprosy reaction, a patient develops painful red nodules on the face, extensor limbs, and trunk along with fever, neuritis, and orchitis. ESR is elevated and biopsy shows panniculitis with neutrophilic infiltrate. What type of reaction is this?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (Type 2 reaction) occurs in LL and BL leprosy. It is an immune complex–mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction characterized by painful nodules, fever, iritis, neuritis, and orchitis. Treatment is thalidomide or clofazimine; NSAIDs for mild cases.

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer presents with an irregular pigmented lesion on the calf that has grown over the past year. Dermoscopy reveals atypical pigment network, blue-white veil, and regression structures. ABCDE criteria show asymmetry, irregular border, variegated color. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Topical imiquimod and review in 3 months
questions.exp: For a suspected melanoma, complete excisional biopsy with 2mm margins is preferred over punch or shave biopsy, to obtain Breslow thickness which guides definitive surgical margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Imiquimod is for superficial BCC/AK, not melanoma.

questions.q: A 70-year-old male with long-standing sun damage presents with a slowly growing pearlescent nodule on the nose with telangiectasia and central ulceration. The Gorlin syndrome (basal cell nevus syndrome) is associated with multiple such lesions and mutations in which gene?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. Gorlin syndrome is caused by mutations in PTCH1 (patched-1 gene), a tumor suppressor in the Hedgehog signaling pathway. TP53 mutations are seen in SCC. BRAF is mutated in melanoma. CDK2A/CDKN2A mutations predispose to familial melanoma.

questions.q: A 38-year-old female with SLE develops photosensitive rash, alopecia, and Raynaud's phenomenon. ANA is positive (1:640), anti-dsDNA is elevated. She now presents with discoid lupus lesions. Which finding on histopathology is most characteristic of discoid lupus erythematosus?
opts: Interface dermatitis with basement membrane thickening and follicular plugging
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) on histopathology shows interface dermatitis (vacuolar/lichenoid), thickened basement membrane, follicular plugging (hyperkeratosis in follicular ostia), and perivascular/periappendageal lymphocytic infiltrate. DIF shows granular IgG/IgM/C3 at DEJ (lupus band).

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash of the eyelids, Gottron's papules over the knuckles, and mechanic's hands. He is found to have anti-Jo-1 antibodies. What is the most important investigation to perform urgently?
opts: CT thorax to look for interstitial lung disease
questions.exp: Anti-Jo-1 antibodies (antisynthetase syndrome) are specifically associated with interstitial lung disease (ILD) in dermatomyositis. CT thorax is urgent to assess pulmonary involvement, which is the main determinant of prognosis and mortality. Mechanic's hands is a clue to antisynthetase syndrome.

questions.q: In a patient undergoing Mohs micrographic surgery for basal cell carcinoma, what is the key advantage of this technique over standard wide local excision?
opts: Faster procedure with no anesthesia required
100% margin evaluation allowing maximum tissue conservation
Can be performed without histopathological assessment
questions.exp: Mohs surgery examines 100% of surgical margins (compared to <1% with bread-loaf sectioning in routine excision), enabling the smallest possible excision with the highest cure rates. It is indicated for high-risk BCC and SCC: recurrent tumors, ill-defined margins, cosmetically sensitive areas, perineural invasion.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for lupus presents for routine evaluation. Which of the following screening investigations is essential to detect drug toxicity?
opts: Annual ophthalmic examination (fundoscopy + visual field testing)
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine causes irreversible retinal toxicity (bull's-eye maculopathy). Annual ophthalmic screening is mandatory after 5 years of use or earlier in high-risk patients (renal disease, high dose >5mg/kg/day, pre-existing eye disease). Early detection by visual fields/OCT can prevent blindness.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with greasy, yellowish scales on the scalp with areas of hair loss and cervical lymphadenopathy. Wood's lamp examination shows green-yellow fluorescence. What is the causative organism and appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Tinea capitis due to Microsporum canis (ectothrix infection from cats/dogs) shows bright green-yellow fluorescence on Wood's lamp. Griseofulvin is the traditional treatment for tinea capitis. T. tonsurans (most common in USA/UK) does not fluoresce. Tinea capitis requires systemic antifungals (topical is insufficient).

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with a painless papule on the frenulum that ulcerates and heals spontaneously. 6 weeks later he develops a diffuse maculopapular rash involving palms and soles with generalized lymphadenopathy. RPR is reactive at 1:64. What is the current recommended treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose
Azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM as a single dose
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis presents with the pathognomonic palm and sole rash plus lymphadenopathy following primary chancre. Treatment is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis. Doxycycline (28 days) is an alternative for penicillin allergy (late latent). Azithromycin resistance is reported.

questions.q: Which statement about Fitzpatrick skin type VI is most accurate in context of laser therapy?
opts: Higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring; longer pulse durations preferred
Lower risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation compared to type III
Same laser parameters as skin type I can be used
Q-switched lasers cannot be used in this skin type
questions.exp: Fitzpatrick type VI (deeply pigmented) has a high risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) and hypopigmentation with laser treatments. Longer pulse durations, lower fluences, and test patches are recommended. Pre-treatment with topical agents (hydroquinone, retinoids) reduces PIH risk. Q-switched lasers can be used with caution.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with grouped papulovesicles on an erythematous base on the penile shaft. Tzanck smear shows multinucleate giant cells. He reports 3 similar episodes in the past. HIV test is negative. Appropriate management includes:
opts: Acyclovir 400 mg TDS for 5 days (episodic) OR daily suppressive therapy if >6 episodes/year
Benzathine penicillin IM weekly for 3 doses
questions.exp: Recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2) management includes episodic therapy (acyclovir 400mg TDS × 5 days or valacyclovir 500mg BD × 3 days) for infrequent recurrences, or daily suppressive therapy for ≥6 episodes/year or with psychosocial impact. Tzanck smear showing multinucleate giant cells supports herpes diagnosis.

questions.q: A 19-year-old female presents with extensive eczema over the flexures since infancy, family history of asthma and rhinitis, elevated serum IgE, and positive prick test to multiple aeroallergens. Which immunological pathway is primarily responsible for the acute phase of this disease?
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) in the acute phase is dominated by Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-13 driving IgE production; IL-31 causing itch). Chronic lesions also recruit Th1 (IFN-γ) and Th22 components. Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling and is highly effective in AD.
